781.quote_or_event: “I am without a protector, O great king; there is nobody to protect me, I know no friend nor any one to have sympathy with me.” … “My own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness; my own Self, friend and foe, according as I act well or badly.”
781.explanation: The young monk Anâthi tells King Śreṇika that no friend or kinsman could shield him from suffering, and that in the end only one's own conduct acts as friend or enemy.
781.tie_back: The Kural calls friendship the rarest gain and the surest guard against enemies, while Jainism holds that the last line of defence is the self, which becomes its own friend by acting well.
781.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.9 and 20.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
781._accuracy_note: Both verses checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The passage is about friendship and protection, but it moves the source of protection from friends to the self, so it is closer to a contrast than a parallel.

782.quote_or_event: “Friendship with the wise, whose intelligence divines our thoughts, is like eating a sugar-cane from the top (as its sweetness increases more and more); connexion with persons without sweetness of disposition is like eating it from the opposite end (the flavour decreasing by degrees).”
782.explanation: The Jain Tamil quatrain contrasts a friendship with the wise, which grows sweeter over time, with one with ill-natured people, which loses its sweetness bit by bit.
782.tie_back: This is the same contrast the Kural draws between the waxing and waning moon: friendship with the good keeps growing, and friendship with fools keeps shrinking.
782.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 1 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
782._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the Indian Antiquary translation on wisdomlib.org. The sugar-cane image matches the Kural's moon image almost exactly in structure; the source is Tamil Jain didactic poetry, not canonical scripture.

783.quote_or_event: “The enjoyment of the friendship of men of acute understanding is desirable as the joys of heaven.”
783.explanation: The Naladiyar compares the company of discerning friends to heavenly happiness, and in the next sentence calls the company of the unlearned a hell.
783.tie_back: The Kural says the friendship of people of good character gets sweeter each time, like a fine book; the Naladiyar likewise counts the company of the wise among life's highest delights and ties it to learning.
783.source: Naladiyar, ch. 24 'Improper Friendship', stanza 3 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
783._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against wisdomlib.org (first sentence of the stanza only). The theme of delight in worthy friends is shared, but the Kural's central image of rereading a book and its sense of growing delight are missing; Tamil Jain text.

784.quote_or_event: “As the virtuous Kitra, for old friendship's sake, loved the king who was attached to sensual pleasures, and as he had at heart his welfare, he spoke to him the following words”
784.explanation: The monk Kitra, who had been King Brahmadatta's companion through several past births, meets him again and, out of that old friendship, bluntly warns him that his pleasures lead to suffering and urges him to give them up.
784.tie_back: The Kural says friendship exists to step forward and rebuke a friend who goes too far, and Kitra does exactly that, speaking against his friend's excess because he cares about his welfare.
784.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.15 (Kitra and Sambhûta; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
784._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com, where an OCR error prints the verse number as '(is)'; it is verse 15. A strong narrative match for rebuke out of friendship, though in the end the king ignores the advice.

785.quote_or_event: “Men cleave not to those to whom their hearts cleave not, within a short space of time; but will the friendship which cherishes the memory of those who are intertwined with one's heart be abandoned, though they are absent from us for a long time?”
785.explanation: The stanza says friendship rests on hearts bound together, not on time spent together, and that it lasts through long absence.
785.tie_back: The Kural says friendship needs neither frequent meetings nor long acquaintance, only a shared understanding of heart, and the Naladiyar likewise grounds friendship in that bond and not in physical presence.
785.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
785._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against wisdomlib.org. Close match on friendship rooted in the heart and surviving long separation; Tamil Jain didactic text rather than canonical scripture.

786.quote_or_event: “It is better to be without the love of those who are without sincerity.”
786.explanation: The Naladiyar holds that affection that is not sincere is worth less than no affection at all.
786.tie_back: The Kural rejects friendship that only makes the face smile and accepts only the kind that gladdens the heart, and the Naladiyar likewise rejects love that lacks inner sincerity.
786.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 9 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
786._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against wisdomlib.org (opening sentence of the stanza). The outward-versus-sincere contrast is shared, but the Kural's face/heart image is absent; Tamil Jain text.

787.quote_or_event: When the newly ordained prince Meghakumāra, crushed by the burden of self-control, wavered and wanted to give up the monk's life, Mahāvīra stopped him by reminding him of his past birth as an elephant that held its foot in the air to spare a hare. Megha became steady in his vows again, repented and went on with his austerities.
787.explanation: Jain tradition presents the Jina as a guide who heads off a follower's fall at the moment of weakness and sets him back on the path.
787.tie_back: The Kural's friend turns a companion away from ruin and guides him onto the right way, and Mahāvīra does the same for Megha, though the story has no counterpart to the Kural's third duty of sharing in a misfortune that could not be prevented.
787.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Parva 10 (Mahāvīracaritra), 'Part 7: Story of Meghakumāra' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org); the episode is first told in Jñātādharmakathā 1
787._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the outline (elephant birth sparing the hare, Mahāvīra's reminder, Megha becoming firm in his vows again) was confirmed from search excerpts of the wisdomlib.org page of Johnson's translation, not a full reading, and the Parva number is from that page's place in the work. The relationship is master and disciple, not friends, and only two of the Kural's three duties are covered.

788.quote_or_event: “If I stretch not out my hand and deliver my whole soul without hesitation to my friend who is in distress, may I be cast into the hell where the wretch is punished who has violated the chaste wife of his friend, and may I be scoffed at throughout the far-famed earth!”
788.explanation: The speaker swears a solemn oath that he will reach out at once, without hesitating, to a friend in distress, and calls down the worst punishment on himself if he fails.
788.tie_back: The Kural pictures friendship as a hand that flies to catch a slipping garment, and the Naladiyar's friend likewise stretches out his hand without hesitation to relieve a friend's distress.
788.source: Naladiyar, ch. 24 'Improper Friendship', stanza 8 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
788._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against wisdomlib.org. Strong match on immediate, unhesitating help and on the image of the hand, though the Kural's reflex simile of the garment is absent; Tamil Jain text.

789.quote_or_event: “When affection continues affection, then is friendship preserved, like the flower on the stalk, which, being full-blown, closes not again. Those who resemble the lotus, which, having once blown, closes again its petals, know neither affection nor friendship.”
789.explanation: The stanza says true friendship stays constant like a flower that never closes once it opens, unlike the lotus that opens and closes again.
789.tie_back: The Kural places friendship's throne in steady support that never wavers, and the Naladiyar likewise makes constancy without wavering the test of genuine friendship.
789.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 5 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
789._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against wisdomlib.org. Good match on constancy (the Kural's kotpinri), but the Kural's active idea of propping a friend up in every possible way is only implied; Tamil Jain text.

790.quote_or_event: “If after contracting a firm friendship with any one, I set myself to note his good and bad qualities, may I be cast into the hell where the traitor who discovers the secrets of his friend is punished, and may I be scoffed at by the whole world!”
790.explanation: The speaker swears never to audit a friend once a firm friendship has been formed, treating such reckoning as a betrayal.
790.tie_back: The Kural says friendship becomes cheap when friends go around measuring what each is to the other, and the Naladiyar likewise treats keeping score inside a friendship as unworthy of it.
790.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 10 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
790._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against wisdomlib.org. The shared idea, that a friendship should not be weighed up, is only partial: the Kural objects to publicly boasting of closeness, while the stanza objects to privately judging a friend's qualities. Next-best match; Tamil Jain text.
